messages.subject: [R-meta] Question Re: Rma.mv Model
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone -

I have a couple of questions related to a three-level model we plan to
conduct using *metafor. *For context, we have compiled correlations
indexing relationships between cognition and inflammation in the body. We
plan to nest effect sizes (level 1) in sample cohorts (level 2) within
studies (level 3). I wanted to check the following questions:

   1. The literature has different types of correlations. Is it acceptable
   to convert all of these correlations to Fisher's *z *for the models?
   Or, should there way to handle these varying effect size types?
   2. I could not find information in the *metafor *documentation about
   conducting sensitivity analyses for rma.mv objects. Is this possible? If
   so, how?

Thanks in advance,
Tori


-- 
*Tori Pe?a, Ph.D. *(she/her/ella)
Lecturer of Psychology
Director, FaM Lab <https://ptori.github.io/famlab/>
Department of Psychology
Stony Brook University
[image: Stony Brook University logo]

*Note. *I honor and respect boundaries around work/life balance. Please
feel no pressure to respond if you receive my email outside your working
hours.

> I have a couple of questions related to a three-level model we plan to
> conduct using *metafor. *For context, we have compiled correlations
> indexing relationships between cognition and inflammation in the body. We
> plan to nest effect sizes (level 1) in sample cohorts (level 2) within
> studies (level 3). I wanted to check the following questions:

>    1. The literature has different types of correlations. Is it acceptable
>    to convert all of these correlations to Fisher's *z *for the models?
>    Or, should there way to handle these varying effect size types?

You can use the standard r-to-z transformation on all kinds of correlation coefficients. However, the sampling variance equation 1/(n-3) only applies when converting Pearson product-moment correlations with the r-to-z transformation. For other types of correlation coefficients (Spearman, (point-)biserial, tetrachoric, (semi)partial, and so on), it would not be correct to use 1/(n-3) as the variance.

Using the delta method, one can compute the variance of any r-to-z transformed correlation coefficient as long as one has an estimate of the variance of the correlation coefficient to begin with. For example, say you have a study that dichotomized both variables of interest and reports the results in terms of a 2x2 table (how many people scored above/below the cutoff on the first variable versus the second variable). Say this is the 2x2 table:

       Above  Below
Above  15     5
Below   8     18

Then we can get the tetrachoric correlation with:

dat <- escalc(measure="RTET", ai=15, bi=5, ci=8, di=18)
dat

      yi     vi 
1 0.6397 0.0258
 
(this estimates the correlation between the underlying continuous variables). I can now r-to-z transform this with:

transf.rtoz(dat$yi)
[1] 0.757601

But

1/((15+5+8+18)-3)
[1] 0.02325581

is NOT the sampling variance of the transformed tetrachoric correlation. Using the delta method, we can compute a correct (i.e., consistent) estimate of the sampling variance:

conv.delta(yi, vi, data=dat, transf=transf.rtoz, replace=TRUE)                                                     

      yi     vi 
1 0.7576 0.0740

Note that the variance (0.0740) is more than 3 times larger than the incorrect estimate (0.0233), because we lost information from the dichotomization of the two variables and having to reconstruct the correlation from that information. You can actually skip the whole conv.delta() thing since escalc() can directly do all of this for you:

dat <- escalc(measure="ZTET", ai=15, bi=5, ci=8, di=18)                                                            
dat                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                     
      yi     vi 
1 0.7576 0.0740

The same principle applies to other correlation coefficients. Note that the r-to-z transformation is only a variance stabilizing transformation for Pearson product-moment correlations, not for (most) other types of correlation coefficients. However, using the transformation can still be advantageous, since raw correlations are bounded which can result in skewed sampling distributions. The r-to-z transformation can then help to normalize the sampling distributions.

>    2. I could not find information in the *metafor *documentation about
>    conducting sensitivity analyses for rma.mv objects. Is this possible? If
>    so, how?

What type of sensitivity analyses are you thinking of?

> Thanks in advance,
> Tori
>

> Lecturer of Psychology
> Director, FaM Lab <https://ptori.github.io/famlab/>

> Stony Brook University

messages.body_plain:
With respect to sensitivity analyses:

Many sensitivity analyses involve the typical kinds of choices one has to make when conducting a meta-analysis (or really any kind of analysis). Gelman and Loken used the metaphor of "the garden of forking paths" to describe this idea (not in the context of meta-analysis but more broadly):

Gelman, A., & Loken, E. (2014). The statistical crisis in science. American Scientist, 102(6), 460. https://doi.org/10.1511/2014.111.460

Simmons and colleagues call this "researcher degrees of freedom":

Simmons, J. P., Nelson, L. D., & Simonsohn, U. (2011). False-positive psychology: Undisclosed flexibility in data collection and analysis allows presenting anything as significant. Psychological Science, 22(11), 1359-1366. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797611417632

Of course, none of this is new. The idea that one has to make many decisions, judgments, and choices in collecting and analyzing a set of data is completely apparent to anybody who has ever been in this situation. In the meta-analytic context, this was discussed already early on; for example:

Light, R. J. (1980). Synthesis methods: Some judgment calls that must be made. Evaluation in Education, 4, 13-17. https://doi.org/10.1016/0191-765X(80)90002-6

Wanous, J. P., Sullivan, S. E., & Malinak, J. (1989). The role of judgment calls in meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 74(2), 259-264. https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.74.2.259

And more related to the choices around the statistical methods:

Mengersen, K. L., Tweedie, R. L., & Biggerstaff, B. (1995). The impact of method choice on meta-analysis. Australian Journal of Statistics, 37(1), 19-44. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-842X.1995.tb00869.x

Describing all these kinds of choices and decision points would take too long and some of this is specific to a particular project. But typical choices and judgment calls include:

- eligibility: which studies, outcomes, time points, and populations to include.
- effect-size definition: which effect measure to use and how to compute it; also which effect size to extract when there are multiple reasonable options (e.g., adjusted vs unadjusted odds ratio).
- data handling: dealing with missing information, multiple outcomes, multiple groups, and dependent effects.
- model choice: equal/common-effect vs. random-effects; potentially multilevel/multivariate models.
- estimation: estimator for heterogeneity, inference method, confidence/prediction intervals.
- heterogeneity: how to assess it and which moderators/subgroups to examine via meta-regression or subgrouping.
- study quality: how risk of bias and/or study quality are evaluated and how they enter the analysis.
- Outliers/influential studies: whether and how to identify and handle them.
- Publication bias: which diagnostics and adjustment/sensitivity methods to use.

Hence, there isn't a sensitivity() function. Instead, you have to think about these choices, their potential impact, and which ones you think need to be examined (which is yet another choice - it's INCEPTION all over again). You do this by going down the alternative path in the garden to see what happens (e.g., what happens when I DO remove the non-randomized studies? what happens when I assume a pre-post correlation of 0.7 or 0.1 instead of 0.4? what happens when I exclude this or that study?).

Best,
Wolfgang
